summary: Redwood team demoed the Console's request-storage toggles, redaction pipeline, and the policy-to-toggle matrix. Customer focused on mapping legal retention rules across product flows (claims intake, fraud triage). Discussed hosted vs private tradeoffs and a small pilot using sandbox toggles and PII classifiers.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-25 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Elena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Jules Han (Redwood Product), Priya Shah (Rivermark Head of Data Privacy), Tom Ellis (Platform), Marina O'Neal (Security Architect), Dave Kline (Product)

Optional auto-summary: Quick demo of the Console toggles, walked through CSV-based policy mapping, showed keystores/KMS integration notes, and agreed to sandbox pilot.

[00:00] Elena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Um we have about 45 minutes, we wanted to run through how Redwood's request storage toggles map to policy, and show a couple of examples specific to claims intake. Marco's going to drive the Console walkthrough and Jules will show the policy matrix import.

[00:22] Priya Shah: Thanks, Elena. For context, we have regulatory retention windows across CA and NY for PII — claims need to be kept 7 years in some cases but redacted after 90 days for operational analytics. So we're really trying to understand how toggles map to legal policy.

[00:40] Marco Diaz: Totally, that's a common pattern. I'll share my screen. Quick note: this is a sandbox with pseudo data. The Console page we'll look at is under Settings -> Request Storage -> Policy Matrix.

[01:05] Tom Ellis: Is the matrix something we edit in the UI or can we commit it via Git or CSV?

[01:12] Jules Han: Both — UI for small edits, CSV import for ops. The template includes columns for product_flow, retention_days, redaction_profile, encrypt_at_rest (KMS boolean), kms_key_id, and fallback_variant (hosted/dedicated/private).

[01:34] Marina O'Neal: Quick question, when you say redaction_profile, is that a static replace or a classifier-driven scrub? We need deterministic PII removal for audit.

[01:44] Marco Diaz: Good callout. The profile can be either static regex-based masks or Redwood's PII classifier pipeline which runs a probabilistic tagger then applies structured transforms. For compliance we expose audit logs showing which regex matched or which classifier token spans were removed. Note: classifier has confidence scores and we persist that in the audit log.

[02:05] Priya Shah: Do those logs ever contain the raw PII? We can't have raw email addresses escaping into logs.

[02:12] Marco Diaz: By default, request-level logs for redaction are stored as events with masked snippets, we do not persist raw PII. For private deployments with HSM/KMS you can opt-in to ephemeral secure logging for debug with strict access control, and everything's encrypted with your KMS key. For hosted accounts we support customer-managed keys (CMK) via our KMS integration.

[02:40] Dave Kline: Walk us through a typical toggle: say claims-intake form, we want text generation (for triage suggestions) but we don't want to store full request bodies longer than 30 days. How do we actually set that?

[02:52] Marco Diaz: In the matrix row for claims-intake you set request_storage=ephemeral (0 days), telemetry=aggregated (30 days), and set redaction_profile=claims-strict. We also recommend enabling prefix caching only for non-PII fields to keep latency benefits but avoid persisting PII in the KV cache.

[03:15] Priya Shah: You mentioned KV cache — can that persist PII inadvertently?

[03:21] Marco Diaz: It can if the application sends PII into the model prompt without any tagging. Two mitigation paths: one, use structured request schemas and tag PII fields as non-cacheable; two, use the Console's request-filtering rules which strip or hash fields before they hit the runtime. There's also an automatic PII-detection step that can route requests to a more guarded path (private variant) if PII confidence is high.

[03:48] Tom Ellis: How does routing to a private variant affect latency? We have strict SLAs for triage.

[03:55] Marco Diaz: It depends on deployment. Hosted private variants that live in the same region add negligible network hop, but dedicated/private on-prem can add 50-150ms depending on infra. You can configure canary fallbacks: prefer hosted for latency but failover to private when policy dictates retention or when redaction confidence is low.

[04:18] Elena Park: One thing we often recommend is a hybrid policy — keep the default flow low-latency hosted with aggressive redaction and short telemetry, but route sensitive requests to dedicated capacity where you can enforce egress controls. That gives a good balance of cost and compliance.

[04:34] Priya Shah: Can you show the Console toggle UI please?

[04:40] Marco Diaz: Yep. (pause) Here — row-level toggles. You can set: request_storage options [persist, ephemeral, encrypted-ephemeral], retention-days numeric, redaction-profile dropdown, kms-key select, and an optional pre-send transform script. Also you can attach a YAML policy reference ID that ties back to your legal policy document.

[05:05] Marina O'Neal: Pre-send script — where does that run? On Redwood side or in our VPC?

[05:12] Marco Diaz: On-hosted it runs in a sandboxed runtime in Redwood's control plane (no raw PII persisted), but for Private/VPC we can run it inside your VPC as a preprocessor so the raw payload never leaves your network. There's an option for encrypted proxy execution for on-prem.

[05:37] Dave Kline: How granular can these rules get? Per route? Per token? Per user?

[05:42] Jules Han: The matrix supports product_flow -> route pattern -> environment -> user_role scoping. For token-level we have a token filter mapping but for most customers route-level is sufficient. You can attach dynamic predicates too (e.g., if request.user_role == 'audit' then retention 365).

[06:05] Priya Shah: About the audit trail — if we redact PII, how do reviewers see enough context for QA without exposing PII?

[06:12] Marco Diaz: We provide an audit-mode view where redacted spans are shown with token-level context and confidence scores. You can optionally grant reviewers time-limited access to a decrypted ephemeral view tied to an HSM key with a TTL — that requires an approval workflow.

[06:35] Tom Ellis: Let's talk backups and archiving. If we set retention to 7 years for claims, do you store in long-term archive or is it returned to us?

[06:44] Marco Diaz: You can choose: long-term encrypted archive in Redwood storage (with KMS keys) or an export hook to push records to your S3/GCS bucket. For regulated stuff we usually recommend pushing to the customer's archive so you control egress and retention lifecycle.

[07:05] Priya Shah: Ok, show me a CSV import example.

[07:10] Jules Han: Here's a sample CSV rows snippet: "product_flow,route_pattern,retention_days,redaction_profile,kms_key_id,request_storage" followed by: "claims,\/v1\/claims\/create,90,claims-strict,alias/rv-kms-claims,encrypted-ephemeral". You can upload in the Console and we validate against schemas. If there are conflicts the UI surfaces diffs and a three-way merge helper.

[07:45] Priya Shah: The three-way merge — does it require manual approval? We need an audit of who changed policy.

[07:52] Marco Diaz: Yes, policy changes can be gated by RBAC and an approval workflow; we keep an immutable changelog with diff, user, timestamp. That shows in Audit -> PolicyChanges.

[08:07] Tom Ellis: Slight tangent — what's the developer UX for toggles on the API? We need programmatic control for feature flags.

[08:13] Marco Diaz: Great question. All the Console toggles map to API flags. Example: include header X-Redwood-Request-Policy: claims-ephemeral, or a query param ?policy=claims-ephemeral. The SDKs support attaching policy ids to requests as metadata.

[08:33] Priya Shah: Any limitations on batches? We use batching for throughput. If one item in a batch contains PII should the whole batch be routed to private?

[08:41] Marco Diaz: By default the batching engine is PII-aware: it checks each item and splits batches if necessary. There's a config to either split or fail. Splitting keeps latency for non-sensitive items.

[08:55] Dave Kline: How do we test and validate policies before going live? We can't have accidental retention on production.

[09:01] Jules Han: The sandbox environment includes a policy simulator. You feed sample payloads and it will show what the effective toggles are, which transforms run, and produce a simulated audit log. We recommend creating a test suite of sample messages for each flow.

[09:20] Priya Shah: Can that simulator handle PII fuzzing? We need to test edge cases like embedded PDF text or base64 attachments.

[09:27] Marco Diaz: The simulator supports attachments and will run the same classifier pipeline; for large attachments we recommend pre-extracting text in your pipeline and sending the extracted text to the simulator. We're also working on an attachments plugin that runs in VPC for heavy workloads.

[09:45] Tom Ellis: Security question: SSO and role mapping for the approval flow — do you integrate with our existing SAML/Okta groups?

[09:53] Marco Diaz: Yes, SAML/SSO is supported and we map group claims to roles. We also support SCIM for user provisioning and have RBAC primitives for policy approval steps.

[10:05] Priya Shah: What about data egress protections — can the runtime block calls to external connectors?

[10:12] Marco Diaz: There's an egress policy control that can restrict external tool calls from model outputs, and we can disable outbound connectors per environment. That helps prevent exfil through plugins or tool calls.

[10:28] Dave Kline: Let's walk a concrete scenario: claim #453 has a SSN in the text. The flow is triage->fraud_model->human. What's the recommended path?

[10:36] Marco Diaz: For SSN we recommend: 1) pre-send mask on ingest (hash the SSN field), 2) route to the 'sensitive' policy which uses dedicated variant with encrypted-ephemeral storage, 3) run PII classifier and structured redaction that replaces SSN with token <SSN_HASH:x> and keep the mapping only in your customer archive, 4) for the human step provide a time-limited decrypted view via the approval workflow.

[11:02] Priya Shah: If the mapping is in our archive, how do we reconcile searchability for fraud analytics without exposing raw SSN?

[11:09] Marco Diaz: Use reversible tokenization inside your gateway or a hash-based pseudonymization where the search uses hashed tokens. Redwood supports passing through hash tokens for indexing while keeping raw decryption keys in your HSM.

[11:25] (interruption / slight crosstalk)

[11:30] Tom Ellis: Back to the matrix — show us how to set a per-environment override. We want prod to be stricter than staging.

[11:36] Marco Diaz: On that CSV you can include environment column. In the UI there's an 'overrides' tab that shows environment precedence. Staging can inherit from defaults but prod override can lock a field so it requires approval to change.

[11:54] Priya Shah: Are there any logs that would contradict data residency? We operate primarily in us-east and need to ensure EU claims stay in EU region.

[12:02] Marco Diaz: Yes you can pin flows to region via the routing policy. The matrix allows region column, so requests matching eu/* get served from eu-region endpoints. We also offer data residency guarantees in Private deployments.

[12:18] Dave Kline: What's the expected engineering effort to get our claims flows instrumented? Rough estimate.

[12:24] Elena Park: For a pilot we typically see 2-4 weeks of integration: policy mapping, a few SDK changes to attach policy ids, and test payload creation. For a full rollout depends on number of flows but often 6-8 weeks.

[12:36] Tom Ellis: Pricing question: does encrypted-ephemeral storage have a premium?

[12:41] Elena Park: Yes there's a small premium for encrypted-ephemeral because of the HSM + KMS usage and the ephemeral key rotation. We'll include that in the pricing pack.

[12:50] Priya Shah: Can you show an example of the audit log for a redaction event?

[12:55] Marco Diaz: Sure. (scrolls) Example event: {timestamp, policy_id, route, redaction_profile: 'claims-strict', matches: [ {type: 'email', span_start: 34, span_end: 49, method: 'regex'}, {type:'ssn', span_start: 120, span_end: 131, method:'classifier', confidence:0.97 } ], action: 'redacted', reviewer_id: null}. Note: in UI we present masked snippets not raw text. (transcription note: curly braces sometimes mis-copied in the live export)

[13:35] Priya Shah: Does your audit log keep the classifier confidence? That matters for dispute investigations.

[13:39] Marco Diaz: Yes confidence scores are persisted as part of the event and surfaceable via Audit API.

[13:46] Tom Ellis: Can we run an automated regression check to ensure new model versions don't change redaction behavior?

[13:51] Jules Han: Absolutely — Redwood Optimize hooks can run eval suites that include redaction tests. If a model update causes increased PII leakage we can trigger regression alerts and automatic rollout pause. We also version transforms and classifiers so you can pin them per-policy.

[14:10] Dave Kline: Ok, show me a failure-mode: what happens if the KMS key is temporarily unavailable?

[14:16] Marco Diaz: We have fallback policies: fail-closed (reject requests requiring decryption), fail-open (not recommended), or route to a fallback hosted variant with less strict crypto but still encrypted at rest. Fail-closed is the default for most compliance customers.

[14:33] Priya Shah: For fail-closed, how is the client notified? 4xx vs 5xx? We need observable errors to triage quickly.

[14:40] Marco Diaz: We emit a 503 with a specific error code and an audit event. Console alerting can trigger PagerDuty.

[14:50] Tom Ellis: Let's demo an end-to-end flow — sending a test payload to the sandbox with SSN and show the simulated audit and policy application.

[14:57] Marco Diaz: Running now. 

[15:05] [15:05] Marco Diaz (live demo): Sending sample payload -> simulator result: Policy applied: claims-ephemeral, Redaction applied: SSN masked, Telemetry: aggregated 30 days, Routing: hosted-preferred with private-fallback. Simulated audit attached.

[15:25] Priya Shah: Hmm I see the redaction used classifier but confidence shows 0.81. We'd like threshold 0.9 to trigger private route. Is that configurable per policy?

[15:33] Marco Diaz: Yes threshold is a policy field: pii_confidence_threshold. If confidence < threshold the request can be forwarded to private variant or flagged for manual review.

[15:45] Dave Kline: Is this threshold for entire document or per entity?

[15:49] Marco Diaz: Per entity. You can set entity-specific thresholds.

[16:00] Tom Ellis: A bit about integrations — how does the webhook for audit export handle high throughput? We expect thousands of events per minute.

[16:08] Marco Diaz: Our audit export supports batching and durable retries. For very high throughput we recommend pushing to your SQS/Kinesis endpoint; we also have native S3/GCS export connectors.

[16:20] Priya Shah: On the topic of long-term storage, can we retain only metadata while purging the text? We want to keep policy IDs, spans, and hash tokens for analytics but not the raw text.

[16:29] Marco Diaz: Yes that's a common pattern. The matrix has an 'archive_mode' option where you can persist metadata-only. We also support PII-erase pipelines that replace raw text with indexed tokens before archival.

[16:46] (small pause)

[16:50] Priya Shah: A compliance detail — do you provide QSA-ready evidence for retention windows? We need tamper-evident logs for audits.

[16:58] Marco Diaz: We provide tamper-evident audit logs with chained hashes and signature metadata. For Private deployments you can configure the signing key to be your HSM.

[17:10] Tom Ellis: About the SDKs — we are primarily node and go. Any caveats?

[17:14] Marco Diaz: Node/Go/Java SDKs all support attaching policy metadata and handling the simulator. The only caveat is for browser-based clients you should proxy requests through your backend to avoid exposing keys and to ensure PII tagging.

[17:28] Dave Kline: Let's talk timeline again — after the sandbox proof, what's the pilot success criteria?

[17:34] Elena Park: Success criteria typically: 1) no PII leakage in evaluation suite, 2) acceptable latency (within agreed SLO), 3) policy automation validated via simulator, 4) security review sign-off. We'll codify these in the pilot statement of work.

[17:52] Priya Shah: Any mention of licensing for the classifier models? We have legal concerns about model provenance.

[17:58] Jules Han: We document model provenance in the model catalog. For privacy-sensitive flows we recommend using audited open models or private model variants and we provide model hashes + verification metadata.

[18:12] (brief break in audio)

[18:20] Tom Ellis: A question on costs: you mentioned costs for dedicated and encrypted-ephemeral. Can you ballpark for a mid-sized pilot (~100k requests/day)?

[18:28] Elena Park: We'll follow up with a tailored quote but very roughly, hosted with aggressive redaction and 30-day telemetry is moderate cost; adding encrypted-ephemeral and private routing increases per-request charge by ~12-18% depending on KMS ops. Dedicated is a fixed monthly commit with lower per-request unit costs at scale.

[18:47] Priya Shah: For the pilot we want a mix: triage on hosted, fraud windows on private. Can we set auto-escalation rules by risk score?

[18:55] Marco Diaz: Yes, risk-based routing is supported. You can set a numeric threshold that when exceeded triggers routing to a private workflow or manual review queue.

[19:08] Tom Ellis: Show the manual review queue integration — we use ServiceNow for tickets.

[19:13] Marco Diaz: We have connectors for ServiceNow and Jira. The manual review queue can auto-create tickets with the audit link and TTL for decrypted view.

[19:25] Priya Shah: A red-team thought — if an internal engineer can request decrypted views, how do we enforce least privilege?

[19:32] Marco Diaz: Approval workflow integrates with SSO groups and can require multi-approver for sensitive categories. All decrypted access is logged and tied to user and approval chain.

[19:45] Dave Kline: Ok good. Anything else on the console side?

[19:50] Marco Diaz: One more feature: policy diffs can be scheduled to roll out during maintenance windows and we surface a preflight summary of affected routes and expected audit volume.

[19:59] Elena Park: Let's capture open items — Priya will share policy documents, Marco will spin up sandbox, Elena will send security pack.

[20:10] Priya Shah: Quick question on test data — can Redwood provide synthetic claim examples?

[20:15] Marco Diaz: We have a synthetic data generator tuned to insurance claims patterns; we can provide a seed set. It randomizes PII while preserving structure so you can validate redaction rules.

[20:30] Tom Ellis: Any gotchas around tokenization? We saw earlier that tokenization differences can change redaction spans.

[20:36] Marco Diaz: Yeah tokenization differences across models can shift spans. We store both character offsets and token offsets in the audit event to help reconcile. Also version the tokenizer with the policy so behavior remains stable.

[20:55] (small chatter)

[21:05] Priya Shah: If we run the pilot and find redaction recall is low, can you tweak the classifier thresholds and run a new eval?

[21:12] Marco Diaz: Yes, the classifier tunables are part of the pipeline and we can iterate during pilot. We recommend keeping each change tied to an eval run recorded in Optimize.

[21:26] Dave Kline: Suppose we want the ability to push policy changes via our CI pipeline. Is that possible?

[21:31] Jules Han: Yes the API supports policy mutations and you can put the CSV in your repo; using our CLI you can import from CI and require approval gates for prod promotion.

[21:43] Tom Ellis: Ok show us the CLI workflow quickly.

[21:47] Marco Diaz: CLI example: redwood policy apply --file claims-policy.csv --env staging --approve false. That uploads and runs validations; then you can open a PR in the Console for human approval.

[21:59] Priya Shah: For the audit log retention of the log itself — how long do you keep it and can we TTL lower?

[22:06] Marco Diaz: Audit log retention defaults to 365 days but you can set retention per-policy; for PCI/PII you may want longer immutable retention — we support up to 7 years in archive mode.

[22:22] (brief pause)

[22:28] Marina O'Neal: Any more on encryption at rest? We need FIPS 140-2 compatible ciphers for certain data.

[22:34] Marco Diaz: For Private deployments we can enable FIPS-compliant crypto stacks. Hosted can support FIPS keys via customer HSM integrations depending on region; we'll validate specifics in the security pack.

[22:50] Elena Park: We're approaching the last third of the session — will jump to Q&A and next steps.

[22:58] Priya Shah: One last legal hook — can Redwood help produce the mapping doc between legal retention clauses and toggles? That's what our counsel will want.

[23:05] Elena Park: Yes we'll help produce a policy mapping template and map your clauses to the toggle matrix as part of the pilot onboarding.

[23:18] Tom Ellis: Any tests we should run immediately? We can start with the simulator and the synthetic payload set.

[23:24] Marco Diaz: Exactly, simulator + synthetic dataset. We'll also run the regression suite against your edge cases.

[23:36] (unclear speaker) - filler noise

[23:40] Priya Shah: Can you confirm the sandbox will have the policy simulator and audit export to our S3?

[23:47] Marco Diaz: Yes, we'll provision sandbox with S3 export and sample ServiceNow connector.

[23:55] Dave Kline: A quick note: our compliance team will ask for the chain-of-custody for the audit logs. Make sure that's included.

[24:02] Elena Park: Noted, we'll include chain-of-custody details in the security pack.

[24:10] (small back-and-forth on calendar scheduling)

[24:20] Priya Shah: Anything about third-party model hosting? We sometimes use external vendors for fraud models and want to ensure no cross-contamination.

[24:28] Marco Diaz: You can define isolation groups and egress controls; third-party models can be executed in a sandboxed connector with no persistent storage.

[24:40] Tom Ellis: Ok good. I'm comfortable with the pilot plan.

[24:45] Elena Park: Great — recap of next steps in chat. We'll share the security pack, sandbox access, and the toggle CSV template. Marco will follow up with provisioning ETA.

[24:58] (meeting winds down, final pleasantries)

[25:10] Priya Shah: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the sandbox.

[25:14] Elena Park: Thanks all, we'll follow up by EOD with links.

[25:20] (call ends)

Note: timestamps are approximate. Transcript contains typical transcription errors (mis-named configuration keys, partially garbled code snippets) consistent with a real Fireflies export.
